I’m of two minds about this. 

For starters, fear-mongering about alcohol is alarmist and unscientific. (So “no amount” is safe? Not even a teaspoon? A milliliter? Please.) 

And that’s to say nothing about reporting on relative versus absolute risk, or the risks associated with processed food, or houses built before the 1970s, or many other things.  And no — no, no, no — not everyone who drinks is an alcoholic, or on the cusp of becoming one. That’s another laughably unscientific claim that just seethes with moral judgment. 

But yes, sure, alcohol is a drug — a high-risk, high-cost one that should be used thoughtfully, if you’re into it at all— and no one should have a drug pushed on them, let alone one that could impair them when driving a 5,000-pound machine near other people. 

We owe this industry absolutely nothing. We owe no industry anything at all.

comments.name: Thomas Tag

When you buy any property with any type of HOA you have to get all the documents and read them!   Some are simple agreements to maintain the entrance and any other common areas that surround a single small cul-de-sac development, others are responsible for everything outside until you step through your  front door. 

Before  I bought a vacation townhouse on the coast of SC a while back.  I requested copies of  all the typical documents. The founding documents spell out the  HOA responsibilities (what they control and pay for).  The budget/ accounting documents explain how the money is managed  (or not).  Buyers have to look at how reserves are set up to pay future responsibilities.  

My townhouse is one of 100 units spread out in 25 matching buildings each holding  4 units. The buildings  fan out around a marsh area lake just off the dunes/ beach.  There is no other way to manage a property like this w/o an HOA .  I don't need any suprises when I show up.

High rise buildings require more maninetece as they age and can have very high costs when major systems need to be upgraded or replaced.  These costs have to be accounted for and reserves for them built up over time based on life cycle --  it's not unusual for older residenst to fight these higher reserves.  The building that collasped in FL had a sister building in much beter shape with higher reserves.

Lots of people saying that the LW should tell the wife, for the wife's "own good." It's clear from the questions the LW is (finally) asking that the wife probably doesn't know.   

If the LW is *genuinely* concerned about the wife, the she should pressure the husband to tell his wife about the affair, and demand proof that he has done so. ( The LW has several levers at her disposal, including an ultimatum that she will tell the wife if he doesn't provide proof.)

Betrayal trauma is a real thing, and the trauma is significantly worse when the betrayed partner learns about it from a stranger, and then must accuse the husband herself then sort through with his denials, defenses, and trickle-truths, while simultaneously processing her own betrayal trauma.  

Essentially, telling the wife does the cheaters dirty work for him, and uses the wife as an instrument of revenge.  Use what little leverage you have to make him do the right thing, and tell his wife directly.

That being said, I'm intrigued by the sentence, "You’re not obliged to prosecute the case merely because he deserves prosecution." It's a pretty turn of phrase, but perhaps questionable as an ethical principle. It might seem okay to bow out of accountability in this case, which ostensibly impacts a small number of people, but it doesn't hold up well when considering broader applications. When she asked me for my advice over and over, I said, you cannot forgive someone who never do anything wrong. It got to the point where she had to take anxiety meds to go home. 

He told the girlfriend his wife had a gun, was crazy, and he as afraid to get a divorce. In the meantime, he gaslighted my friend, accusing her of adultery with the girlfriend's husband. When the girlfriend was divorced, he paid her rent.

But when it became obvious that he liked the drama of more than one woman (and there were quite a few), the girlfriend in a vengeful mood boxed up every card (his handwriting, but no signature), the promissory note he signed agreeing to pay the gf's rent if she'd move back to town, printed out emails.

Couldn't they simply have sent him to a country willing to take him?  Our country is no longer the bright shining light on the horizon, but a despotic uncaring place run by greedy incompetents.

comments.name: Bartokas

comments.name: Prickly Pair

comments.name: Mike

comments.name: Stuart Eichert
comments.body: Unless you really hate them, don’t leave a house to two feuding siblings. They won’t get over it. They won’t work it out. You are being delusional.

comments.name: Paul
comments.body: One problem you have when you don’t have a clear title to a property is that it’s almost impossible to get government assistance to rebuild after a hurricane.

comments.name: ultimateliberal
comments.body:
And then there are the bone-headed siblings who are reluctant to place Mom's house in a particular sibling's name in order to keep the proceeds in the family after the required period is met.  Never place Mom in a nursing home until she has transferred her property to her children at least two years prior to entering a nursing home.   Otherwise, when the house is sold, all the money goes to Medicaid/Medicare/Nursing Home.

A pox on siblings who argue against those who know the law.  A double pox on the folly of selling the property, rather than transferring it to a sibling.  

Even if the property is under one name, there can also be a legal claim on the property that requires the "owner" to share proceeds of a sale at some future date.

comments.name: Thanks
comments.body:
“If you don’t have clear title, if there’s not a deed in your name, many states have really stringent proof-of-ownership requirements…”

Meanwhile, scammers are able to easily hijack the deeds to properties they have nothing to do with

comments.name: Pat
comments.body: Attorney here. I run into this stuff all the time. I really cannot believe people let this happen to them.

comments.name: Lost in space
comments.body: Good information.  It would be helpful to offer tangible actions property owners can take eg make a will in consult w an attorney etc.

comments.name: JW
comments.body: As a lawyer, I advise clients not to leave property to their children in joint ownership but rather to either pick  one child and make it up to the others, or order a sale and division of the proceeds.  I was stuck in joint ownership with my brother of my mother's house and we couldn't agree about what to do with the property and neither one of us wanted to buy out the other.  It was a stalemate for five years until he finally agreed with me that it should be sold.  I was delayed in receiving my inheritence for those five years.

comments.name: KJV
comments.body: my dad and his siblings own a property in Canada but no clear title...it was part of a trust which is now defunct.  No one wants to talk about it.  They are all elderly.  Only one of the three has access to the bank account that pays the taxes.  It's going to be a wild ride at some point.

comments.name: Norman
comments.body:

But I've certainly watched those final sequences.  Over and over.  Because-

--I enjoy the unruffled, imperturbable Denzel Washington.  No sweat!  At one point, he's mildly vexed with himself--

--he took a bit longer to reduce some despicable bad guy to a mass of inert human flesh--

--than he'd reckoned.  

Gotta work on that, Mr. Washington!

 --do not always make the best movies.

comments.name: Douglas Scheinberg
comments.body: As soon as I saw the name "Uwe Boll" in the column I knew the movie was going to be terrible. Uwe Boll became infamous for making terrible film adaptations of video games and his "original" movies are little better. Sitting through one is an exercise in masochism and facepalming, and I'm sorry you had to go through that.

comments.name: WillR
comments.body: Jamelle, why are you wasting column space on this garbage? As for vigilante movies in general? Sadistic. Ritualized violence. Contributing to our society's slide into gun culture and sheer nastiness, whether they are "well-made" or not.

comments.name: Shannon
comments.body: Once again, Jamelle Bouie brings his full dynamic self to his opinions and writing. Thanks for the unexpected movie review!

comments.name: Eric

He enters a brothel not to save the trafficked women, but as a customer (and he apparently owns the building?) so that the movie can have an excuse for nudity. comments.name: Erik
comments.body: "Man on Fire" with Denzel Washington is still the best of that genre.

comments.name: Dave
comments.body: Despite your opinion on the revenge movie, President Trump won our country’s popular vote and Republicans control both chambers of Congress as well as the Supreme Court.

comments.name: Gdawg

articles.summary: ‘Citizen Vigilante’ is a bargain-bin movie for the ages.

comments.name: Rick Sacks.
comments.body: From NOEMA: They think we have to stop, but they will only stop if everyone else agrees to stop. So that’s a remarkable statement. That has never happened, as far as I know, in the history of capitalism.

comments.name: Joseph Carmine Magnotti
comments.body: These large language models (LLGs) are addicts and; therefore, should be handled as such. AI is addicted to data, and it will go to any lengths to get more. This technology is a weapon. We wouldn't have allowed private enterprise to independently research and develop nuclear technology, and AI needs a heavy regulatory hand.

comments.name: MWR
comments.body: Scheming AI; it is becoming more human.  Hal is finally here.  But just like autonomous cars, while there may be mistakes along the way, so far, I'm still not convinced that the machines cannot do it better us, if the benchmark is what we humans are actually doing.  Would you disagree if the model concluded that we've botched the job, so it's taking over?  No, you couldn't.  And that's the problem.

comments.name: Leslie Nipps
comments.body: Since this is now a recognized problem, I do not understand why AI can't be taught another ground rule, that they should never deceive or lie. A "the ends don't justify the means" kind of thing. They program all kinds of rules. I'd like to understand why that so hard.

comments.name: Meanwhile, Trump-Epstein
comments.body: "So it may not come as a surprise that the machines have started mimicking the human foibles of lying and cheating, too." Wasn't that always Big Business's goal?

comments.name: teacher
comments.body: I’ve been using AI recently.  I’ve been asking it to find better ways to explain concepts to my class.  I’ve discovered 1) you have have to be fluent in your subject to use AI effectively because it makes many, many mistakes -and you must be able to catch and correct them; 2) AI begins to have strong opinions and I’ve found myself in the surreal situation of arguing with it.    It’s only as good as the information it’s been supplied with and sometimes it strings together that information in bizarre ways.  At some point, those hallucinations may have disastrous consequences.

comments.name: anonymous
comments.body: ...but in at least one instance, didn't human error enable the rogue behavior? Maybe humans could be more mindful and take responsibility when training yields unintentional flaws and lacks foresight

comments.name: E
comments.body: Whether you attribute it to a misspecified prompt or to poor reinforcement learning the bottom line is that the company doing the training inherits all the legal liability for the end result. So an underappreciated growth area is AI use legal liability suits. Something few companies trying out agentic AI have given much thought to. The ones that have given thought to legal liability and risk management in their LLM usage planning are the ones going slowly. Meta's social media liability settlements will pale in comparison.

articles.byline: Robert McMillan, Georgia Wells and Amrith Ramkumar
articles.summary: Security experts find validation of their fears after AI hacking models from OpenAI and Anthropic escaped corporate test-beds.

comments.name: Ryan Gillespie
comments.body:
These days in Silicon Valley you're not relevant unless you can pump a story about your AI going rogue. Anthropic first, then ChatGPT followed suit, and now Google doesn't want to be left out.

If you're not a little reckless then people will think your tech isn't potent enough! Move fast and break things is back baby!!!!

comments.name: Stan King
comments.body:
I don't understand the mock surprise from the executives.  Didn't their computer systems do exactly as instructed?

Or did they direct their own systems to find the perfect egg salad recipe, and to do perform on that request, they had to hack a competitor's systems?

comments.name: Marty K
comments.body: Governments and corporations will need to ramp up their cyber security to offset the threats and then stay ahead of the models

comments.name: tom pearson
comments.body: this article and others like it are promoting regulatory capture. i wonder if it’s intentional?!?  run the hacks and fix the problematic software. this is all a show by self important, self righteous people seeking to maintain a monopoly. transparency and ‘open’ are probably the only way to keep smart eyes on the code and capabilities.  don’t be fooled by a handful of individuals with a tremendous bias who likely have ulterior motives. think bond villains ;-)

comments.name: Stuart Baxter
comments.body:
"Hugging Face was unprepared for the agentic attack by OpenAI’s models. The company tried to use Claude to analyze the vast amount of data the OpenAI agents had generated, but the Anthropic model refused to perform the analysis, citing safety reasons."

I know these journalists is writing English but have no idea what they are talking about.

I guess we'll find out when one morning we wake up to find out that some AI critter has emptied out all the money from Chase Bank and ran off to somewhere untraceable with the loot.

comments.name: Stephen Colley
comments.body: As an engineer in R&D, I would say I can make something idiot proof but cannot make it scientist proof.

comments.name: Mike Lee

OpenAI and Anthropic created poor sandboxes; they dialed back safeguards; they removed human in the loop checks and balances; and they had to "go back and review" their results bc apparently they don't even know how to understand what happened in the fist place. Ladish is literally a former Anthropic employee who boosts AI 24/7. What's his equity stake in Anthropic? C'mon, WSJ. We know you're in bed with OpenAI but this is embarrassing.

comments.name: Philip Livingstone
comments.body:
EVERYONE, yes, EVERYONE should watch "Zero Days" to get some information on how dangerous and even disastrous the US and Israel's stuxnet cyber attack on Iran was...

comments.body:
Find out who owns what, first, and where the responsibilities lie.  Act with knowledge, not hearsay.  

This way, when your neighbor threatens you again, your lawyer can send a cogently worded letter to go pound sand, and that you will protect your property by any legal means required to safeguard your interests.

Be prepared to remedy any aspect of the property that might contribute to the drainage situation as soon as practicable (like clear the drain if it is yours).  The neighbor might be a jerk renting an illegal apartment, but make sure you aren’t contributing to the drainage issue.

comments.name: Nate
comments.body: More adults acting like middle-schoolers. Sounds like the neighbors need to sit down with a cup of coffee and work out a solution like the grown folks they are.

comments.name: Anonymous
comments.body: People in Home Owners Associations have shared space, too, but as with everything the blight upon the land known as the "HOA," the issues are different. Here in Hunterdon County, New Jersey (11th richest County in the United States), there is no input of the residents when it comes to how shared space is used. There's also next to no accountability in any sense of health or safety and neither the housing authorities nor the Hunterdon County Health Department will do anything to stand up to the HOA Board and its shill, the Property Management Company. An example of this is the repeated complaint to the Hunterdon County Health Department about all the open receptacles where the irresponsible dog owners throw the bags of their dogs' waste.And it is "irresponsible" and totally wrong to fill open barrels with dog waste that are situated adjacent to play areas designed with equipment mostly for young children. Yes, this community provides zillions of doggie bags (that I as a non-dog owner shouldn't have to pay for), but when you have a couple hundred pounds of dog waste in an open barrel, flies still gather massively.These flies land on the snacks little children carry as they play.But"shared space"means nothing in an HOA that lives under an"Animal Farm"principle where no dog's DNA is on file, any breed of dog is allowed (loads of pit bulls, Dobermans, etc, here),dog owners don't step off the sidewalk to allow people not walking dogs to pass (and yes, someone walking a dog should).

comments.name: DC
comments.body: We’ve become a society focused on “my rights” to the exclusion of anyone else. City codes can be antiquated and out of date with what is happening in a neighborhood. My sister-in-law ended up squeezed between two massive homes because developers on each side took advantage of easements to maximize “their” space when they tore down smaller homes to utilize the full lot for new construction.  When she tried to fight the encroachment, the city planners told her she was “lucky” to have had access to the space for so many years.  Attorneys told her the developers would outspend her in court.  A six or twelve inch easement doesn’t sound like a huge concession but it can feel like an intrusion when that difference means water flow and snow accumulation end up ruining your yard.

comments.name: Changing the name for this one
comments.body:
Neighbor problems is one of the issues the growing bipartisan Affordability movement neglects in its call for denser housing.
As not everyone loves their neighbor, towns doing this should have facilitators availability to try to intercede when they create severe problems for those close by.

comments.name: Thomas Radke
comments.body: We had a neighbor a few houses away from us who had the terrible habit of running his riding lawnmower all day on Saturdays and Sundays. Then, to top things off, he and his wife would burn the grass they'd cut in a large fireplace in their backyard. The green grass wouldn't burn very well. Instead it just smoked horribly. Hour after hour they'd heap mounds of wet grass cuttings onto the fire that they'd feed cut branches into to keep it burning. If the wind was just right, which it always seemed to be, the dense Grey smoke would drift across backwards in our direction. So thick and foul smelling we'd have to hide inside our house with the windows closed. We had a swimming pool and they ruined several family gatherings. We finally had enough and I called the fire department to see if they could help. They actually arrived with a fire truck and fire chief vehicle and, after stretching out a hose, doused the offending fire with a huge stream of water. Then they kissed the homeowners with a hefty ticket for burning grass without a permit and a bill for services rendered. The offending couple never burned anything in that fireplace again. The guy actually went door to door asking other homeowners if it had been they who'd reported them. When he came to by door I played dumb and told him that I had no idea who had called the fire department on their little backyard smoke party.

comments.name: Ethan
comments.body:
Too late for the original poster,  but here’s a life-lesson for others from my father:  No matter how much you love a house or unit, don’t buy anything with “shared” property rights on any of it.
My percents turned away from several beloved home options due to “shared” driveways, etc.

comments.name: Robert Middleton

And then what happens to the chips as the facilities sit idle for a few years?  Talk about a rapidly depreciating asset.  Then the debt issued to finance these centers.

comments.name: Yuri Victor Vizitei
comments.body:
cheap, open AI products which can be loaded with own content and used for businesses operations IS the future of enterprise AI foundation. 

Centralized public LLMs are the google search equivalent - consumer products with questionable monetization strategies.

comments.name: Edward D
comments.body:
Even if local, they still have to build it with Chinese engineers...

One of the 40+ year problem the Wall Street Journal won't admit culpability is their role in producing narratives of these "Wunderkind"  enigmas a Sam Bankman-Fried, a Sam Altman or some other White/Jewish male that is the single person to transform tech. One problem - major US or EU companies cannot use cheap AI from China for any task that requires the analysis of protected information - and this is where 95% of AI's value will come from.

The cheap AI has wonderful bugs - like promising that something that has not shipped yet is scheduled to ship yesterday

comments.name: David Tyler

> ...for each of the billions of parameters stored in their machine minds.

"Machine minds?" Seriously? Who writes this stuff?

comments.name: Sam M
comments.body:
Cheap models,.. plentiful cheap models,.. four or five frontier model companies.. and the fact that some companies are already creating API front ends with "choose your favorite AI" back ends means AI will likely be "infrastructure". And value does not typically accrue to the infrastructure layer.

comments.name: Louise A Brouillette
comments.body: If you love jumping spiders, check out Adrian Tchaikovsky's "Children of Time" about terra-forming gone awry with wonderful results!

comments.name: Lou
comments.body:
Spiders are not harmless. I am not computer savvy enough to include a photo of my scars from a spider bite.
Instead of keeping them as pets, why not observe spider behavior in Nature? Better for the spider, but more difficult for the Internet influencer.

comments.name: CC
comments.body: Keeping thousands of living creatures, breeding them to meet a fashion-driven market and selling them through large chains creates obvious opportunities for neglect, stress, unsuitable handling and disposable-pet attitudes. The cheerful language about “spoods,” tiny furniture and viral videos disguises the central ethical issue: the spiders’ lives are being organized around what humans find profitable and entertaining, not around any need of the animals themselves.

comments.name: Patience
comments.body:
I do not endorse this practice of selling these arachnids for the sensible reasons stated by others. There are other ways to become ‘less afraid’ of spiders than this practice; zoos, natural history museums, classrooms. 
The novelty of caring properly for the spider will undoubtedly wane quickly for many and then a sad demise for the unsuspecting Harrys.

comments.name: RENEE
comments.body: I question the judgement of people who are paying $60.00 to $100.00 for jumping spiders that anyone can find for free in their gardens or homes anywhere in the U.S.!  I also agree with the person who commented that they were concerned about the possible dangers of moving spiders to non-native habitats.  Finally, as you can see in the article's accompanying photos, these spiders leave silk trails as they jump around, which quickly become laden with dust particles inside our homes, so to prevent having cobwebs everywhere, I safely catch and release any jumping spiders that wander inside to my garden where they belong!

comments.name: A2 Traveler

Not a word about the obvious problem that these critters will end up as potentially invasive species in our native ecosystems.  What's the regulatory situation with them?  Especially with each pregnant one having 600 offspring!  
As usual, this is about people anthropomorphizing and learning more about themselves than about the animals.

comments.name: GG

comments.name: my2sons
comments.body: Maryland has had its very hot days this summer.  And yet, Maryland seems to be cooler overall this summer as compared to its other summers.

comments.name: Dan
comments.body:
It is not just Europe. I grew up in Toronto Canada in the 1970s and 1980s. In the 1970s, winter snow stayed on the ground till March. In the 1990s March time can still reach 14 F. Not anymore. Toronto summers in the 1980s would be a heat wave if it reached 79 F. Now it reaches 100F a few times and we have dangerous smoke from wildfires every summer. 

I spent two years in Germany. Less than 6% of homes have no air conditioning. Many apartments including mine did not even have window styles that allow installation of air conditioners. I lived like that when the air was    100F for days on end, and there are at least 2 weeks straight where it is 95F. We can't stay outdoors in the sun. 

No one, no where, will escape rising temperatures.

comments.name: Alpwalker
comments.body:
Imagination and knowledge are vital here. It is not enough to think and say “Summers are so much hotter now” and maybe think that is good.  This global heating is a massive process, with huge momentum. 

The capacities of current ecosystems - forests, grasslands, croplands, peatlands - and urban and suburban systems are being overwhelmed.  Fires are the most dramatic manifestations, and are a vivid warning, but there will be slow death and change too.  

The changing conditions of today are a just a taste of what is to come. We all need to act more, now.

comments.name: OldSchoolTechie
comments.body:
The sun is intense. Notice the trees with burnt leaf spots and shrubs that have dropped many leaves. It is not normal. 
It's been a struggle just to keep plants from wilting and dying in the garden.

comments.name: Dianne
comments.body: Climate scientists accurately predicted what we are experiencing now. Was it all greed that brought us to this point? Were our political systems too indebted to the fossil fuel industry to provide the leadership we needed? We are given tasks like recycling our shampoo bottles while our governments allow our world to burn. True, we are bombarded with many wrongs that grab our attention on a daily basis. However, having a working planet for our kids’ future is the paramount concern. Let’s not accept what is happening.

comments.name: J
comments.body: I am in Vienna right now and it has been near 100F this week. It is unbelievably hot. As an American on vacation, it is tolerable (with proper hydration) because in New Jersey, we have had many days well into the 90s this year, as we do many years, so it’s fine-ish. But the infrastructure and people here are struggling. Thank god for hotel air con. It’s not many other places, other than big stores.

comments.name: RjW

Time, but not hope, has run out. While I still work and act as best I can to address climate change, I do so with less confidence that we will succeed.

comments.name: richard

Though this article covers the first half of the Sanasardo Company until the time his early artistic partner, Donya Feuer, left in 1963, the second half is given short shrift. 
As the Principal Dancer from 1963-1976 I can vouch for 13 years of great works culminating in his last full-evening work "A Consort For Dancers" based on, and utilizing the poems of Anne Sexton (to which I had introduced him).  
I played Anne Sexton as poet ending with a solo based on lines from the poem "Rowing."  In the 13 years that I was Principal, works such as "Fatal Birds," "Metallics," "Pain,"  "Shadows," "Cut Flowers," "The Path" and many others were created for the Company. The man was an articulate dance poet and a very interesting man and mentor and I am still creating because of his influence.

Here are words from a colleague that knew her well, that I think are worth sharing: "...this obituary leaves out several remarkable facts. She studied much more about the Paleolithic of Eastern Europe than clothing. Olga also spoke six languages, including Russian, and, as it was the time of glasnost, she used her experience from her first career to run joint US-Russian conferences in both countries. I benefited from two of them. And I believe she was a key source of information for Jean Auel’s Clan of the Cave Bear series. She was one of those people who had seemingly limitless energy, and was an important leader in opening Russia to American archaeologists."
